site.name: Tomoshibi Atlas
site.tagline: Physical and mental health, the challenges facing AI (SI), IT and social systems, and the support available — on one globe.
purpose.title: About this site
purpose.body: Public information on outbreaks, mental health, welfare and research, cyber threats, disasters and crime — on one globe, to help people prepare.
purpose.relation: "Lights" are information about the systems that support people's health and daily lives. "Warnings" are information that needs attention: threats to the IT and AI that run those systems, and disasters and crime. For example, if a hospital's or a welfare office's systems are shut down by a cyberattack, the care and support themselves stop. "Research & Response" also includes results achieved with AI and official security, disaster and crime prevention measures. Where documents such as those of the US government call AI "SI" (Super Intelligence), the site treats them as AI information.
guide.title: Purpose & how to use
guide.howto.1: The globe rotates slowly. Drag to rotate; use the mouse wheel or two fingers to zoom.
guide.howto.2: Use the tabs at the top to switch topics. Tap a light or a headline to open the information for that area, with links to the original sources.
guide.howto.3: Search for a country or area, or press "My location", to move the globe there and stop.
guide.howto.4: When you select a country, ripples spread across the nearby sea. Reading pages can be switched to a light mode with the button at the top right (nothing is saved in your browser; it lasts while you move around the site).
guide.legend.1: Large headlines: items highlighted by fixed rules, such as recent publication (this is not a severity rating)
guide.legend.2: Faded "earlier report": a newer report exists for the same area and topic. Kept visible until 7 days after its own publication date
guide.legend.3: The dark side of the globe is where it is currently night; the faint orange band is around sunrise or sunset. On a larger screen such as a computer, you can see the stars clearly on the night side
guide.support: Support the site (optional; it does not change what you can use)
caption.outbreak: Infectious diseases: WHO Disease Outbreak News, retrieved automatically twice a day. Each light marks a country named in the report.
caption.research: Research & Response: from peer-reviewed papers and public bodies — research in medicine and AI (SI), official IT and AI security updates, and official disaster and crime prevention measures, added after checking the original. NASA and NIH headlines are retrieved twice a day.
caption.care: Mental health & Welfare: mental health statistics and support services, and the systems that support daily life with the challenges noted in official reports. Added after checking the original; statements about challenges reflect the cited source.
caption.security: IT security: alerts from public bodies (US CISA, JPCERT/CC, IPA), retrieved twice a day. Each light marks the publishing agency's country, not where an attack occurred or came from.
caption.crime: Crime prevention: warnings and statistics on scams, fraud and other crime from public bodies, added after checking the original, plus automatic headlines from public bodies abroad.
caption.disaster: Disasters: Not a source for emergencies. Damage reports on typhoons, heavy rain, heat, fires and more from public bodies, added after checking the original (Japan's FDMA headlines are retrieved twice a day).
caption.quake: Earthquakes: Not a source for emergencies. Magnitude 5.5+ worldwide (preliminary USGS data, retrieved twice a day; while this section is open, your browser also loads the latest list).

add.title: Welfare guides, security steps and more
add.welfare: Welfare: the site also lists official places to ask for help in each country. Choose the Mental health & Welfare tab and select your country on the globe or by search; a list organised by type of problem appears at the bottom. For Japan, a separate page lists consultation services by topic and by prefecture, plus links to official disaster information (the Japan Meteorological Agency, hazard maps and each prefecture's disaster page).
add.welfareBtn: Find your country in the Mental health & Welfare tab
add.security: IT security: besides threat information, the site will add steps that individuals using computers and smartphones can take, based on information from public bodies.
add.securityBtn: See security steps you can take
add.research: How mental health, infectious diseases and research connect: countries and international bodies are working on using AI and other tools to detect illness earlier, spot early signs of outbreaks and advance drug research (in Japan, for example, research developing AI to help detect depression earlier has been selected for public funding [FY2021 examples]). At the same time, there has been a case in Japan where a hospital's systems were stopped by a cyberattack and it suspended new outpatients. This site lets you switch between these research developments (Research & Response), the infectious diseases and mental health concerns actually occurring, and the security of the IT that supports them (IT security), while staying on the same region.
add.sources: Basis: WHO (2021 report on AI in health; 2021 Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence), AMED (FY2021 programme on implementing AI in medicine), Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (2022 material on a cyberattack on a medical institution). Sources are listed on the About page.

meta.description: Tomoshibi Atlas (ともしびアトラス, "Atlas of Lights") is a non-profit site run by Yutaka Yoshioka (吉岡有隆). It shows public information on infectious diseases, mental health and welfare, and medical research alongside AI (SI) and IT security threats and earthquake, disaster and crime-prevention information on one globe, with official links to support services in each country.

next.title: What you can do next
next.outbreak.1: Check the original (such as the WHO report) for the date, the countries or areas concerned, and later updates.
next.outbreak.2: If you plan to travel, check the infectious disease information for your destination and quarantine guidance before you leave.
next.outbreak.3: If you feel unwell after returning from a trip, phone a medical facility before visiting and tell them where you travelled and for how long. In an emergency or if you need urgent care, call emergency services right away (119 in Japan).
next.outbreak.4: Before sharing unconfirmed claims seen on social media, compare them with announcements from public bodies.
next.research.1: Check in the original whether it is a peer-reviewed paper, an announcement by a public body or a developer announcement (the nature label on each item is a guide).
next.research.2: Research results cannot necessarily be used as treatments or products right away. Ask a doctor or pharmacist about treatment and medicines.
next.research.3: For security updates, check whether the products you use are affected and update them following the developer's official instructions.
next.research.4: For striking headlines, check the subjects, period and conditions in the original.
next.care.1: When things are hard, do not carry them alone: talk to a support service or someone close to you.
next.care.2: Statistics describe society as a whole, not individuals. Do not use them to blame yourself or people around you.
next.care.3: Eligibility and contact points can change, so check the official page before applying.
next.security.1: Check whether the products and services you use are affected.
next.security.2: Update from the developer's official website or the product's own update feature, not from links in e-mails or text messages.
next.security.3: Do not contact links or phone numbers shown in suspicious e-mails or fake warning screens.
next.crime.1: Share the tricks with your family and people close to you.
next.crime.2: If you are told "guaranteed profit", "pay now" or "we can recover your losses", end the contact and do not decide alone.
next.crime.3: In Japan, you can consult the police consultation line #9110 or the consumer hotline 188.
next.disaster.1: Follow the information and instructions of the government and local authorities.
next.disaster.2: Check the risks where you live on a hazard map, and decide where to evacuate and how to contact your family.
next.disaster.3: When donating, choose channels introduced by local authorities or public bodies, or organisations whose operators you can verify.
next.quake.1: Epicentres and magnitudes include automatically determined values and may be revised later (the "Preliminary" label).
next.quake.2: After a large earthquake, stay alert for further earthquakes and check the latest information from local authorities.
next.quake.3: Prepare in advance: secure furniture and keep water and food in stock.

guide.spaceBody: A slow journey away from the Earth, past the Moon and the Solar System to the Milky Way. It is a place to look at the Earth from a little further away when everything in front of you feels like too much. When you come back, it says "Welcome home." It loads only when you press it, so the rest of the site stays light.
